item.title: 664 thousand books, dozens of agents — and not a single metric can be trusted
item.description:
I need my own book canon. A canon is a single stable record of "this text" to which everything else is attached: files in different formats, audiobooks, editions, duplicates. Not because external sources are bad. If I need to quickly get the author, title, or identifier of a book, I can easily get it from an existing catalog. Even if the catalog has garbage, it's not a disaster: garbage can be gradually fixed. The problem is different — it's not my catalog. I can spend years accumulating the results of my own analyzers around an external identifier: linking audiobooks to it, finding duplicates, identifying editions, collecting statistics, building recommendations. And then the external source will change identifiers, structure, or simply disappear, and all the accumulated work will hang in the air. Therefore, I decided to create my own corpus of books. It will also be dirty, and that's okay. The main thing is that it's my dirty corpus: I can gradually improve it, and I control its identifiers myself. The corpus currently contains about 664 thousand books. And the task for which all this was needed, at first glance, was very simple: take a few minutes of an audiobook, run it through Whisper, and find the corresponding book by text. What could be difficult? It turned out — almost everything. Read more

item.title: Why LLMs Need a "Harness": How to Turn an LLM into a Working AI Service
item.description:
A large language model can be downloaded from Hugging Face, deployed on a server with a GPU, and sent its first query. Technically, the LLM is already working: it receives text input and generates a response. But it's still a long way from a ready-to-use business service. Users need an interface. Applications need an API. The model needs to be fed context and corporate data. Access to the service must be restricted, actions controlled, queries logged, and errors handled. For the model to do something useful for the business, it will need to be provided with context, connected to external or internal systems, and have its operating rules defined. All these components around the model are often called a harness. In this article, we'll explore why it's needed, what parts it can consist of, and why choosing the LLM itself is just one step in creating an AI service. Read more

item.title: Why Decisions Made in Meetings Don't Turn into Tasks: Meeting Minutes and Diffusion of Responsibility
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Georgy, and I lead sales and marketing at Aspro.Cloud. I have over fifteen years of experience in B2B sales – TELE2, Samsung, Whirlpool, managing teams of up to fifty people. The meeting ends on time. Everyone nods, leaves with the feeling that they've agreed. A week later, it turns out no one called the client. Five people heard the task in the moment, and each, deep down, decided someone else would handle it. Sound familiar? It has a name and nearly sixty years of research behind it, though no psychologist in 1968, of course, was thinking about Zoom meetings. Read more

item.title: Where AI Models Get Top Companies From: 62% of Answers with Links Contain Someone Else's Compilation
item.description:
I analyzed AI model responses to questions containing the words 'best,' 'top,' and 'rating' to see where the lists came from. Out of 208 responses with source links, 130 (62%) contained a pre-existing compilation: someone's top-10 list, rating, or comparison. The responses were gathered across 32 projects in various niches, from accounting outsourcing to fulfillment, totaling 368 responses with links in 208 cases. Getting into an AI model's answer largely depends on getting into the compilations the AI finds. At the end, I explain how to check your niche with 3-5 questions and what to do with each compilation found. Read on.

The integration with the SourceCraft development platform, which we launched in 2025, helped understand code directly within the article. The feature appeared directly in code snippets: click the button, and the AI assistant explains what's happening in a specific code fragment, considering the article's context. item.title: The Most Destructive Technological Transition in History
item.description:
I'm only 44, but I remember a world without the internet, mobile phones, navigators, and messengers. To call my future wife, I had to run to a payphone on the street and drop a coin into the machine. To find something out, I'd go to the library and open the Great Soviet Encyclopedia, a sort of paper Google, but without ads, comments, or the ability to diagnose yourself with a fatal illness in three minutes. I drove around the city without a navigator. And somehow, miraculously, we managed to meet friends at a precisely appointed time on the other side of the city, without the ability to share geolocation or text "I'm almost there" when I hadn't even left the house yet... It was an amazing time. We easily embraced new technologies and adapted to them quite quickly. The internet, mobile communication, computers, smartphones – all of this entered our lives gradually, giving us time to get used to it. But now the pace of change is completely different. Are we still sure that we will adapt to everything next just as easily? Although, I fear, we don't even have a clue what awaits us. And this time, we might not be given time to get used to it. No, I won't write about AI suddenly going out of control, starting to improve itself, and outsmarting humanity in a matter of months. Most likely, there will be no robot uprising at all: we are simply handing over control of business, the economy, the army, and the state to algorithms step by step, because AI decisions turn out to be more effective than human ones.
